Chapter 9: The Long Road to Healing
Healing from the deep wounds of war and torture... it’s never simple, is it? There aren’t any shortcuts, or magic words that make the pain go away. For a lot of people, that journey toward healing starts with something as basic—and as brave—as telling the truth. Just admitting what really happened, to yourself and maybe, if you’re ready, to someone else.
I want you to picture this: a former interrogator, weighed down by guilt, finally reaching out for help. Those first therapy sessions? They’re tense, filled with awkward silences and half-spoken thoughts. But slowly, the words start to come. He talks about the pressure he felt, the fear, and those moments when he just... lost track of himself. He shares the nightmares, the crushing shame, and this deep longing for forgiveness.
It’s not easy—it hurts. But it’s also a relief. For the first time, he feels like someone actually sees him. Not as a monster, but as a person—someone who’s made mistakes, but wants to make things right. The therapist doesn’t judge, and doesn’t make excuses. They just listen. And that, more than anything, changes everything.
Healing looks different for everyone. Some folks find a support group, where they can finally talk to people who truly get it. Others turn to faith, drawing comfort from rituals and the warmth of a community. And a few—well, they become activists, determined to make sure no one else repeats their mistakes.
You know, most people don’t realize just how much courage it takes to face up to the past. It’s so tempting to bury the pain, or pretend nothing ever happened. But real healing? That only starts when you’re honest—with yourself, and with others. When you’re willing to look at what happened, and ask, “What can I do differently now?”
This road to healing is long. Some days, the memories hit too hard. Other days, the anger or the shame just feels like too much. But with time, and with the right support, it is possible to find some peace.
Healing isn’t about forgetting. It’s about learning to live with your past—carrying those memories, but not letting them define who you are. It’s about finding hope again, even after all the things you wish you could take back.
